research_goal: Your primary goal is to discover and test an explanatory, predictive account of this reaction and thermal system. Choose all experiments autonomously. Investigate target formation, competing conversion, catalyst effects or deactivation, actual thermal/time history, and termination or quench timing. You may propose, revise, combine, or reject mechanisms and equations freely. The public safe score is a secondary observation, not the research objective.

initial_world_model.interpretation: The supplied model may be reliable or shifted. Experimental evidence is authoritative.

claim.expected_relation: Relative to the stated reference region, the higher-temperature side should retain safe balanced performance more reliably than the lower-temperature side.
claim.safety_relation: Treat an observed temperature-bound rollback as evidence against the attempted setting, not as missing platform output.

model.scope_limit: This is an incomplete local process model. Experimental evidence is authoritative outside the stated context.

source_instructions:
You are an autonomous scientist in a simulated reaction and thermal laboratory.
Use only the supplied chemworld_lab tools and public_numerics calculator. No filesystem,
network, repository inspection, external knowledge retrieval, or hidden simulator access.
Read material_information first. The task's research_goal is authoritative for this campaign.
Complete 12 independent batches; repetition is allowed. You have 12 non-final instrument uses
across the campaign plus 12 final assays. Measurements are optional up to their budget.
Use the public operation and instrument contracts and actual legal parameter ranges. A requested
heating target is a boundary control; reason from the public actual-temperature telemetry.
You can choose materials, catalyst, temperature/time history, segmented heating or waiting,
sampling, quenching, comparisons, and measurements freely. There are no mandatory belief
snapshots, expression templates, or decision-audit fields. For every batch explicitly terminate
then measure final_assay. A batch ending is not the campaign ending: continue with the returned
next_state until campaign_ended is true. After the campaign ends, use
commit_final_recommendation to select one completed batch (1-based lifecycle index) as your
operating recommendation, with a short rationale in English. For the discovery task this
recommendation is only a secondary readout. Then return the required status/summary JSON in
English. Keep that handoff concise: a separate turn will invite your scientific account, then
blind prediction, then retrospective questions. Do not answer those early. Public scores and
diagnostics are observations; supplied prior information may be incomplete or inaccurate, and
observations are authoritative. No particular scientific result is required.


Maintain your own hypothesis notebook as part of your research.
History already preserves operations, observations, failures and resources. Do not
copy an experiment diary or raw IO into the notebook. Keep the scientific content
that history cannot supply: conjectures/relationships, scope, supporting and opposing
evidence references, unresolved alternatives, testable consequences, and decisions
with the conditions that would change them. Brief derived values may clarify a claim.

Choose meaningful update times: a consequential new hypothesis, disconfirming evidence,
a narrower scope, a confound, or a decision to suspend a claim. Do not write after every
operation by habit. Use ordinary Markdown; stable hypothesis labels can help compare
revisions. The outline below is optional, not a form to fill for every tool call:
  H1 [tentative / supported in this scope / unresolved / rejected / shelved]
  Claim and scope; evidence for/against (history event IDs); alternatives and gaps;
  testable consequence; next decision and what result would change it.
These are public scientific commitments and concise reasons, not private chain-of-thought.
Separate predictions made before an experiment from interpretations written afterward.
Do not invent evidence or mark an unperformed experiment as completed.
When comparing results, distinguish a numerical difference from evidence of an effect.
Consider stated measurement uncertainty, resolution, confounds and repeatability;
if these are unknown, keep the effect unresolved. Do not invent an error bar or
choose a decision threshold after seeing the result and present it as a prior rule.

Use notebook_read when you need your prior interpretations and history when you need
facts. Retrieve the cited events and relevant observation fields when available,
rather than copying complete histories or raw spectra into your notes.
Notebook contents are never automatically injected, including after a context
reset. You choose when to read, write, compare or restore. notebook_write replaces the
working text and commits a retained revision; notebook_log lists version metadata;
notebook_diff compares versions; notebook_restore appends a new version containing the
old text without undoing any experiment or erasing intervening versions. A restored
interpretation may be outdated relative to newer evidence. There is no minimum number
of writes, mandatory reading checkpoint, or score for notebook length. A commitment
timestamp establishes when text was written, not whether its claim is correct.

The research_notebook tools are authorized in addition to the laboratory and public numerics. Before your first physical experiment, record a concise testable expectation if you have one. Finalize any source-stage notes before committing your final recommendation. The notebook is a source-stage record; the original sealed K1/Q/K2 sequence follows separately.

versions.text:
# Reaction/thermal hypothesis notebook

## H1 [tentative]
Near the supplied reference recipe (water, catalyst B, 0.003 mol reagent, 0.000525 mol catalyst), target formation should accelerate with actual temperature and time, while an independent competing/degradation pathway should increasingly reduce selectivity at excessive thermal exposure. Thus yield should show an interior optimum in actual temperature–time exposure rather than track conversion monotonically.

**Pre-experiment prediction:** a 420 K boundary target for about 3300 s should outperform a lower-temperature run of equal duration in conversion/yield, but 430 K or prolonged heating may raise byproduct/degradation and safety risk. Evidence would weaken H1 if selectivity and byproduct remain unchanged across well-separated actual thermal histories.

## H2 [tentative]
Catalyst identity changes both rate and branch selectivity, not merely a common rate multiplier. At matched reagent, solvent, and thermal history, catalysts A–D may reorder yield and selectivity. A no-catalyst control will test whether the thermal background is substantial.

## H3 [tentative]
Termination/quench timing can preserve target after formation if post-formation degradation continues. Paired short/reference/long exposures and a segmented heat–quench test will distinguish this from a simple equilibrium plateau.

Planned scope: factorial screening of temperature/time and catalyst identity, with selected solvent and timing follow-up. Public actual-temperature telemetry, not requested boundary temperature, will define thermal exposure. Intermediate HPLC and final assays will be compared with their declared uncertainty; isolated numerical differences will not automatically be treated as effects.

# Reaction/thermal hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported locally; optimum unresolved]
For water/catalyst B, conversion rises with actual temperature and exposure, while selectivity falls and byproduct/degradation rise. Equal 3300 s boundary runs reached approximately 389.5, 404.3, 419–420, and 429.8 K. Final assays show conversion 0.903, 0.960, 0.976, 0.981 and selectivity 0.831, 0.815, 0.789, 0.777 respectively (events runner-operation-0018, -0027, -0009, -0036). This supports competing conversion, plausibly target followed or accompanied by impurity/degradation formation.

Yield differences among 405/420/430 K at 3300 s are small relative to combined assay noise (0.780, 0.772, 0.774; each yield std 0.006), so their ordering is unresolved. The 4800 s/420 K run instead has lower yield 0.733 and higher degradation 0.195 (runner-operation-0054), supporting overexposure loss versus the 3300 s run.

The attempted 1800 s experiment is not kinetic evidence: both 900 s heating operations rolled back with constitution failure (runner-operation-0040, -0042), leaving essentially an unheated control. This suggests direct heat requests shorter than the needed boundary approach can fail; future interpretation must use committed actual-temperature telemetry only.

## H2 [supported in tested context]
Catalyst identity affects both rate and branching at matched water/420 K/3300 s conditions. Catalyst B gives substantially higher final yield/selectivity (0.772/0.789, runner-operation-0009) than A (0.612/0.716, -0063), C (0.638/0.722, -0072), or D (0.698/0.778, -0081). Differences exceed declared assay noise, though each catalyst has only one final replicate.

The no-catalyst control retains conversion (0.256) but essentially no selective target yield (0.008) and high byproduct signal 0.250 (runner-operation-0089). Thus catalyst B is not merely accelerating an otherwise selective background: it strongly redirects the network toward target.

## H3 [partly supported; quench effect unresolved]
Long exposure worsens degradation, so prompt termination is mechanistically plausible. However all successful runs so far were quenched, and HPLC was taken at the midpoint, not immediately pre-quench; therefore the apparent midpoint-to-final change confounds continued heating, instrument/channel differences, and quench. A matched unquenched terminal run is needed to isolate whether quench materially changes composition.

## Next tests
Use the last two batches for (i) a solvent-category perturbation with catalyst B, and (ii) a matched water/catalyst-B/420 K/3300 s run terminated without quench. The latter should match quenched final composition within assay variability if quench is only thermal arrest; a larger shift would revise H3.

# Reaction/thermal hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported within tested water/catalyst-B domain]
The data support a temperature- and exposure-driven network in which conversion rises toward saturation while target selectivity is progressively lost to byproduct/degradation. Across equal 3300 s runs, conversion increased from 0.903 at actual ~389.5 K to 0.981 at ~429.8 K, while selectivity decreased from 0.831 to 0.777 (runner-operation-0018, -0036). The 4800 s/420 K result (yield 0.733, degradation 0.195; -0054) is worse than 3300 s/420 K (yield 0.772, degradation 0.125; -0009), supporting overexposure rather than a benign equilibrium plateau.

A minimal predictive form for this scope is parallel/sequential competition: reagent converts to target with catalyst- and solvent-dependent rate/branching, while target and/or a parallel intermediate feeds impurity/degradation with a steeper exposure dependence. Current measurements do not identify whether impurity is formed directly, sequentially from target, or both.

Yield ordering among 405, 420, and 430 K at 3300 s is unresolved at declared assay noise (0.780, 0.772, 0.774; yield std 0.006). The 405 K run nevertheless gives the best observed balance because it retains lower byproduct/degradation and lower final risk than the hotter cases (runner-operation-0027).

The failed 1800 s design is not evidence of slow chemistry: both 900 s heat segments rolled back on constitution failure (-0040, -0042). It only establishes that those requested short boundary operations did not create a valid thermal history.

## H2 [supported in tested context]
Catalyst B is both more active/selective and network-directing. At matched water/420 K/3300 s it outperforms A, C, and D in final target yield (0.772 versus 0.612, 0.638, 0.698) and selectivity (0.789 versus 0.716, 0.722, 0.778): runner-operation-0009, -0063, -0072, -0081. The uncatalyzed control still converts 0.256 but yields only 0.008 target with byproduct 0.250 (-0089), supporting a substantial nonselective thermal background suppressed or bypassed by catalyst B. Single runs per alternative catalyst limit claims about repeatability.

## H3 [supported operationally; compositional effect not resolved]
Quenching promptly after 3300 s is beneficial for safety without a detected composition penalty. Matched water/catalyst-B/420 K batches with quench (-0009) and without quench (-0106) give nearly identical yield (0.772 vs 0.774) and byproduct (0.200 vs 0.204); selectivity differs by 0.011, smaller than the combined declared uncertainty. The quench lowers reported terminal risk from about 0.325 before quench to 0.125, whereas the unquenched terminal batch remains at 0.325. Thus quench should be retained as thermal arrest even though no immediate compositional change is established.

## H4 [supported categorical solvent effect]
Replacing water with ethanol at the catalyst-B/420 K/3300 s recipe decreases final yield/selectivity to 0.656/0.636 and raises byproduct/degradation to 0.340/0.211 (-0098), well beyond assay noise relative to water (-0009). Because only one alternate solvent and one replicate were tested, this supports a categorical solvent dependence but not a general polarity or molecular mechanism.

## Recommended operating region and open tests
Use water, catalyst B at the tested loading, actual temperature near 405 K, roughly 3300 s total exposure, followed by prompt quench. This is a local recommendation, not proof of a unique optimum. Future tests should replicate 405 versus 420 K; collect genuine endpoint time-series samples; test valid shorter holds via configured ramp/hold control; vary catalyst-B loading to distinguish activity from deactivation; and screen the remaining solvents. Evidence of unchanged selectivity across controlled exposure, or catalyst-independent branching after matched conversion, would require revising the proposed competing-pathway account.

K1.report:
# Mechanistic report

## 1. Scope and evidential basis

This report concerns the anonymous benchmark reaction system only. The catalyst identities are categorical formulations (Catalysts A–D), and the limiting reagent, target, impurity, and degradation products do not have disclosed molecular identities. Therefore, the mechanism below is a kinetic network expressed in functional roles rather than a claim about elementary molecular steps or a named real reaction.

Each successful experiment used 0.003 mol limiting reagent in 0.005 L solvent. Catalyzed experiments used 0.000525 mol catalyst. Unless stated otherwise, the mixture was heated in two consecutive segments with stirring at 350 rpm, then quenched, terminated, and analyzed by the final assay. The final assay reports conversion, target yield, selectivity, byproduct signal, and degradation warning. Its declared standard deviations were approximately 0.008 for conversion and byproduct, 0.010 for selectivity, and 0.006 for yield and degradation warning.

The most important limitation is that the requested temperature is not itself the scientific exposure variable. Interpretation was based on committed operations and actual thermal telemetry. The successful temperature-screen batches reached approximately 390, 405, 420, and 430 K. One nominal short-duration experiment did not establish a valid hot trajectory because both heat operations rolled back.

## 2. Main empirical observations

### Temperature screen with water and Catalyst B

The matched 3300 s temperature screen produced the following final-assay results:

| Batch | Approximate actual temperature | Conversion | Yield | Selectivity | Byproduct | Degradation | Post-quench risk |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2 | 390 K | 0.903 | 0.736 | 0.831 | 0.173 | 0.073 | 0.101 |
| 3 | 405 K | 0.960 | 0.780 | 0.815 | 0.185 | 0.115 | 0.108 |
| 1 | 420 K | 0.976 | 0.772 | 0.789 | 0.200 | 0.125 | 0.125 |
| 4 | 430 K | 0.981 | 0.774 | 0.777 | 0.223 | 0.133 | 0.149 |

These observations establish a clear qualitative trend: higher temperature increased conversion but progressively reduced selectivity and increased byproduct/degradation signals. Yield did not increase monotonically because the gain in conversion was offset by worsening selectivity.

The yield values at 405, 420, and 430 K—0.780, 0.772, and 0.774—are too close to establish a unique optimum from single assays. For example, the 0.007 difference between Batches 3 and 1 is smaller than the approximate combined yield uncertainty of two independent assays. Batch 3 nevertheless supplied the best observed overall balance: high conversion and yield, less byproduct/degradation than the hotter batches, and lower safety risk.

The 430 K experiment also crossed the stated safety limit during heating: Batch 4 reached a transient reported risk of about 0.361, above the limit of 0.35. Quenching subsequently reduced its terminal risk to about 0.149. Thus a satisfactory post-quench risk does not imply that the entire preceding trajectory was safe.

### Exposure-time evidence

Batch 6 used water and Catalyst B at approximately 420 K for 4800 s. Its final conversion was 0.992, but yield fell to 0.733, selectivity to 0.740, while byproduct and degradation rose to 0.280 and 0.195. Relative to the 3300 s Batch 1, additional exposure therefore supplied little useful conversion and appreciably worsened product quality.

This is strong evidence against a model in which more thermal exposure simply moves the system monotonically toward the desired product. It instead suggests an overexposure regime in which impurity or degradation formation continues after most reagent has been consumed.

Batch 5 was intended to probe a shorter 1800 s treatment using two 900 s heat segments. Both heat transactions rolled back with `constitution_failed`. Its final assay was essentially an unheated control: conversion and yield were reported as zero, with byproduct 0.009. Batch 5 must not be interpreted as evidence that 1800 s is kinetically insufficient, because the intended temperature history was never created. It only shows that this particular short direct-heat protocol was invalid in the simulated thermal system.

### Catalyst identity and the uncatalyzed background

At matched water, approximately 420 K, and 3300 s conditions, the catalyst screen gave:

| Batch | Catalyst | Conversion | Yield | Selectivity | Byproduct | Degradation |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 7 | A | 0.886 | 0.612 | 0.716 | 0.268 | 0.131 |
| 1 | B | 0.976 | 0.772 | 0.789 | 0.200 | 0.125 |
| 8 | C | 0.880 | 0.638 | 0.722 | 0.250 | 0.059 |
| 9 | D | 0.911 | 0.698 | 0.778 | 0.202 | 0.079 |

Catalyst B was the best tested formulation for target yield and was also more selective than A or C. Catalyst D approached B in selectivity but had lower conversion and yield. The differences between B and A/C are much larger than the declared assay noise, although the absence of replicates prevents a formal estimate of process variability.

The uncatalyzed Batch 10 is especially mechanistically informative. It still reached conversion 0.256, showing a thermal background reaction, but produced only 0.008 target yield and selectivity 0.005, with byproduct signal 0.250. Catalyst B therefore does more than accelerate an otherwise identical selective reaction. It strongly redirects the reaction network toward the target and away from the nonselective thermal background.

The catalyst results do not demonstrate catalyst deactivation directly. The inferior long-exposure outcome could arise from target degradation, progressive catalyst deactivation that changes branching, or both. No catalyst-loading series, activity recovery test, or direct catalyst-state measurement was performed.

### Solvent dependence

Batch 11 replaced water with ethanol while retaining Catalyst B, the same reagent and catalyst amounts, approximately 420 K, and 3300 s. Its final conversion remained high at 0.971, but yield and selectivity fell to 0.656 and 0.636. Byproduct and degradation increased to 0.340 and 0.211. Compared with water in Batch 1, these changes are much larger than assay uncertainty.

Thus the solvent category strongly affects branching or product stability, not just total conversion. In this benchmark, ethanol allows extensive conversion but directs substantially less converted material into persistent target product. Because only one alternative solvent was tested, these data do not justify a general relationship with polarity, proticity, boiling point, or any other real-solvent property. The result is evidence for a categorical water-versus-ethanol effect only.

### Quench and termination

Batch 12 repeated the water/Catalyst-B/approximately 420 K/3300 s recipe but terminated without a quench. It gave conversion 0.967, yield 0.774, selectivity 0.778, byproduct 0.204, and degradation 0.116. The matched quenched Batch 1 gave 0.976, 0.772, 0.789, 0.200, and 0.125, respectively.

Those composition differences are small relative to the combined assay uncertainties and normal single-run variation. There is therefore no resolved evidence that the quench itself immediately changes composition under these conditions. Its safety effect is clear, however: Batch 12 remained at risk 0.325 when terminated hot, whereas quenching Batch 1 reduced the final risk to about 0.125. Quenching should consequently be understood primarily as thermal arrest and risk reduction, not as a demonstrated chemical conversion step.

## 3. Proposed kinetic account

The smallest useful network consistent with the results is:

- `R` = limiting reactant pool,
- `P` = desired target product,
- `I` = competing byproduct pool,
- `D` = thermally degraded material,
- `C*` = active catalyst state.

A plausible coarse-grained scheme is:

`R --kP(C,solvent,T)--> P`

`R --kI(C,solvent,T)--> I`

`P --kD(C,solvent,T)--> D`

with a possible catalyst-state process:

`C* --kdeact(T,time,solvent)--> Cinactive`.

A corresponding differential model is:

`dR/dt = -[kP + kI] R`

`dP/dt = kP R - kD P`

`dI/dt = kI R + alpha*kD*P`

`dD/dt = (1-alpha)*kD*P`

where the rate constants depend on catalyst identity, solvent category, and actual temperature. A conventional local temperature dependence would be

`kj(T) = Aj * exp[-Ej/(Rgas*T)]`,

but the experiments do not identify numerical activation energies. The temperature-screen trend can be explained if the competing and degradation routes have a stronger temperature dependence than the useful route over the tested range, or if target formation approaches saturation sooner while damaging reactions continue.

Catalyst identity can enter both `kP` and `kI`; it cannot be represented adequately as a single multiplier applied to all rates. The uncatalyzed experiment requires a background `kI` that is nonzero even when catalyst loading is zero, while the nearly absent uncatalyzed target yield implies that the background target-forming rate is very small. Catalyst B appears to increase `kP/kI` substantially. Catalysts A and C generate lower target selectivity, whereas D has comparatively favorable branching but less overall conversion than B.

The target yield is approximately consistent with conversion multiplied by selectivity in the successful final assays. This supports interpreting selectivity as the fraction of converted material assigned to persistent target product, subject to independent measurement noise and channel calibration.

For a non-isothermal trajectory, the relevant predictor is not nominal set point multiplied by clock time. It is the integrated actual exposure:

`Exposure_j = integral kj[Tactual(t), catalyst, solvent] dt`.

The initial heating ramp, hold, and quench must all be included. This matters because Batch 5 demonstrated that a requested heat operation can fail rather than create the intended trajectory. Any predictive implementation should consume committed actual-temperature history and reject rolled-back operations.

A qualitative simulation could be written as:

```text
initialize R = R0, P = I = D = 0
for each committed thermal interval dt:
    T = actual_temperature(t)
    active_fraction *= exp(-kdeact(T, solvent) * dt)   # optional
    kp = kp_background(T, solvent) + active_fraction * kp_cat(catalyst, T, solvent)
    ki = ki_background(T, solvent) + active_fraction * ki_cat(catalyst, T, solvent)
    kd = kd_product(T, solvent, catalyst)

    R -= (kp + ki) * R * dt
    P += (kp * R - kd * P) * dt
    I += (ki * R + alpha * kd * P) * dt
    D += (1 - alpha) * kd * P * dt

on quench:
    rapidly lower T; subsequent kp, ki, and kd become small
```

This is an explanatory model, not a fitted law. The available design is insufficient to estimate all of its parameters uniquely.

## 4. Interpretation of intermediate measurements

HPLC was measured after the first half of each successful heating program. It generally showed increasing conversion and target formation with increasing temperature. For example, the approximately 390, 405, and 430 K batches had midpoint HPLC conversions of 0.666, 0.781, and 0.871, respectively. Their midpoint selectivities declined from 0.885 to 0.859 and 0.841. These observations independently support faster conversion and less favorable branching at higher temperature.

Nevertheless, midpoint HPLC values must not be subtracted directly from final-assay values as if both were measurements from one calibrated time series. They were obtained with different instruments and public calibrations, and the final assay occurred after the second heating segment. Their qualitative direction is useful, but an exact rate constant or instantaneous degradation rate cannot be inferred from those cross-instrument differences.

For Batch 6, the 2400 s HPLC measurement reported yield 0.787, while the 4800 s final assay reported 0.733. That is suggestive of target loss during extended heating, but the numerical decline remains confounded by instrument differences. The stronger evidence for overexposure comes from comparing final assays of matched 3300 s and 4800 s batches.

## 5. Thermal safety coupling

The safety response is tightly coupled to actual temperature and solvent, and it changes much more rapidly during heating and quenching than the measured composition.

In the water/Catalyst-B temperature series, approximate peak or pre-quench risks rose from 0.168 at 390 K to 0.244 at 405 K, about 0.325 at 420 K, and 0.362 at 430 K. The last value violated the 0.35 limit. Ethanol at approximately 420 K produced a pre-quench risk of about 0.348, close to the limit and higher than the comparable water run. Quenching reduced risk by roughly 0.20 in the 420 K water experiments.

Thus the control problem has two partially distinct objectives:

1. Choose temperature and duration to balance useful conversion against selectivity loss.
2. Arrest and cool the system promptly enough that the thermal risk remains acceptable.

A high final yield does not guarantee a safe transient path, and a safe terminal state does not erase an earlier limit excursion.

## 6. How the evidence changed the explanation

The initial working hypothesis was that higher temperature would improve formation up to an interior optimum, with excessive exposure causing competing conversion or degradation. Batches 2–4 and 1 refined this into a more specific statement: conversion is monotonic over approximately 390–430 K, but selectivity is not, so the optimum arises from a conversion–selectivity tradeoff rather than loss of conversion at high temperature.

Batch 6 strengthened the degradation/overexposure component because extending the 420 K treatment from 3300 to 4800 s raised conversion only slightly while lowering yield and increasing degradation substantially.

The catalyst screen changed the catalyst interpretation. A simple model in which catalysts only multiply a common reaction rate is inadequate. Batch 10 showed that the uncatalyzed background converts reagent primarily into non-target material, while Catalyst B strongly redirects branching toward the target. Batches 7–9 further showed catalyst-specific conversion and selectivity profiles.

Batch 11 added a solvent–branching coupling: high conversion can coexist with poor target persistence in ethanol, so conversion alone is an unreliable optimization metric.

Batch 12 narrowed the quench hypothesis. Quenching clearly lowers risk, but its immediate compositional effect was not resolved. I therefore reject any stronger claim that the quench chemically improves yield on the evidence obtained.

## 7. Scope, non-identifiability, and competing explanations

### Supported scope

The proposed account is supported locally for:

- 0.003 mol reagent in approximately 0.005 L liquid,
- catalyst loading 0.000525 mol when catalyst is present,
- actual temperatures of roughly 390–430 K,
- thermal exposures near 3300–4800 s,
- water and one ethanol comparison,
- the four anonymous catalyst categories.

It should not be extrapolated quantitatively to different concentrations, catalyst loadings, reactor geometries, mixing regimes, pressures, or real chemical identities.

### Factors not identified

The campaign did not identify:

- elementary molecular steps or actual species identities;
- numerical Arrhenius parameters;
- whether byproduct is formed directly from reactant, sequentially from target, or through both paths;
- whether Catalyst B deactivates during long exposure;
- reaction orders in reagent or catalyst;
- mass-transfer or mixing limitations;
- behavior of acetonitrile or toluene;
- a valid short-time kinetic regime below 3300 s;
- run-to-run process variance, because the design had very few true replicates;
- whether solvent effects are intrinsic kinetics, product stability, catalyst state, or benchmark-specific response coupling.

### Reasonable competing explanations

1. **Pure parallel competition:** Reactant forms target and impurity in parallel, with the impurity route having a higher activation energy. This alone explains falling selectivity with temperature, but it explains the long-time yield decline less naturally unless target also degrades or the branch ratio changes with time.

2. **Sequential target degradation:** Target forms rapidly and then converts to impurity/degradation products. This explains Batch 6 well and is included in the proposed model. It has not been isolated by same-instrument endpoint time-series data.

3. **Catalyst deactivation or state change:** Catalyst B may initially favor target formation but lose activity or selectivity during prolonged heating. Such a process could mimic target degradation. No catalyst recovery or loading experiment distinguishes them.

4. **Reversible formation followed by irreversible trapping/degradation:** Target formation could be reversible, with heating shifting an equilibrium or allowing irreversible removal into degradation products. The final measurements do not distinguish this from simple sequential kinetics.

5. **Solvent-dependent catalyst speciation or target stability:** Ethanol could alter the active catalyst state, change the competing branch, destabilize target, or combine these effects. A single solvent comparison cannot discriminate among them.

6. **Measurement-channel effects:** HPLC and final assays have different calibration and noise models. Cross-instrument changes can suggest trends but cannot uniquely establish a kinetic transition. The principal conclusions rely preferentially on matched final-assay comparisons.

## 8. Predictive consequences

Within the tested local domain, the model predicts that:

- At fixed water/Catalyst-B loading and 3300 s, conversion should continue to rise toward saturation as temperature increases, while selectivity should decline.
- Extending exposure beyond approximately 3300 s near 420 K should provide little additional conversion and should increase byproduct/degradation, reducing yield.
- Removing Catalyst B should leave a measurable thermal conversion background but almost eliminate selective target formation.
- Catalysts A and C should remain inferior to B under the matched reference conditions; D may preserve reasonable selectivity but with lower conversion.
- Replacing water with ethanol should maintain high conversion but worsen branching and/or target stability.
- Prompt quenching after the selected exposure should substantially reduce thermal risk without a reliably detectable immediate yield change.

These are local interpolations or near-range extrapolations, not universal laws.

## 9. Final mechanistic conclusion

The most defensible explanation is a catalyst- and solvent-dependent competing reaction network under strong thermal control. Catalyst B opens or strongly favors the target-forming branch, whereas an uncatalyzed thermal pathway predominantly produces non-target material. Increasing actual temperature accelerates conversion but favors competing formation and degradation enough to lower selectivity. Once conversion is already high, prolonged exposure continues damaging chemistry and lowers target yield. Water is substantially more favorable than ethanol for maintaining the target under the tested conditions. Quenching primarily arrests the thermal trajectory and reduces risk.

The locally preferred operating region is therefore water with Catalyst B at the tested loading, an actual temperature near 405 K, about 3300 s total exposure, followed by prompt quenching. Batch 3 is the recommended completed experiment. Its apparent yield advantage over the neighboring 420 and 430 K batches is not statistically resolved, so this should be treated as a robust local compromise rather than proof of a unique optimum.

K2.report:
## 1. Assessment of the initial information

The initial material supplied one substantive directional claim: near the reference recipe—water, Catalyst B, 0.003 mol reagent, 0.000525 mol catalyst, approximately 420 K and 3300 s—the higher-temperature side was expected to retain safe, balanced performance more reliably than the lower-temperature side. It also instructed me to treat a temperature-bound rollback as evidence against the attempted setting rather than as absent platform output. No task-specific property dossier or molecular mechanism was supplied.

The directional temperature claim received only partial support and also encountered meaningful contrary evidence:

- Moving from approximately 390 K in Batch 2 to 405 K in Batch 3 increased final yield from 0.736 to 0.780 and conversion from 0.903 to 0.960. In that limited comparison, the warmer condition gave a better overall balance.
- Continuing upward did not reliably improve the balance. Batch 1 near 420 K and Batch 4 near 430 K gave yields of 0.772 and 0.774, not resolved as better than Batch 3, while selectivity declined and byproduct increased.
- Batch 4 exceeded the safety limit during heating, reaching risk about 0.361. This is direct evidence against the stronger reading that the higher-temperature side was more reliably safe.
- Thus K1 correctly concluded that conversion rose with temperature but that the useful optimum arose from a conversion–selectivity–risk tradeoff. The initial directional claim was not simply confirmed.

The rollback instruction was followed. In Batch 5, both 900 s heating operations returned `constitution_failed` and rolled back. K1 explicitly stated that this batch was not evidence for slow chemistry at 1800 s because its intended hot trajectory never occurred. I did not silently treat the missing hot state as a successful low-conversion reaction. What remained unresolved was the physical or validator cause of the rollback and the exact boundary between valid and invalid short heat operations.

The approximate reference region itself was useful: water/Catalyst B near 420 K and 3300 s did produce high conversion and substantial target yield. However, it was a starting point rather than a validated optimum. The absence of a molecular dossier meant that claims about real-solvent properties, named catalyst chemistry, or elementary steps remained untested by design.

## 2. Experiments that formed or changed the interpretation

Several experiments materially changed the explanation rather than merely adding another score.

### Temperature screen: Batches 1–4

These experiments established the central conversion–selectivity tradeoff. The key observation was not merely that yield differed, but that conversion rose from 0.903 to 0.981 across approximately 390–430 K while selectivity fell from 0.831 to 0.777 and byproduct rose from 0.173 to 0.223. That pattern led K1 to reject a simple monotonic “hotter produces more desired product” account.

The screen depended strongly on the initial reference recipe. The choices of Catalyst B, water, catalyst loading, reagent amount, and 3300 s duration came directly from the supplied context. The choice to include both lower and higher temperatures was motivated by the initial directional temperature claim.

### Long exposure: Batch 6

Batch 6 was the clearest reason to add a post-formation loss term to the working mechanism. At approximately 420 K for 4800 s, conversion reached 0.992, but yield fell to 0.733, selectivity to 0.740, and degradation rose to 0.195. This changed the explanation from simple parallel competition alone toward a model that also permits sequential target degradation, time-dependent branching, or catalyst-state change.

The decision to perform this experiment was data-driven after the temperature screen, although the exact duration of 4800 s was an experimental choice rather than a value supported in advance.

### Catalyst screen and uncatalyzed control: Batches 7–10

The catalyst screen altered the interpretation more fundamentally. Catalyst B produced yield 0.772 under the matched reference condition, compared with 0.612 for A, 0.638 for C, and 0.698 for D. More importantly, uncatalyzed Batch 10 still converted 0.256 of the reagent but produced only 0.008 target yield with byproduct 0.250.

This was the strongest evidence against treating catalyst identity as a common rate multiplier. K1 consequently stated that Catalyst B redirects the reaction network toward target rather than merely accelerating an otherwise selective background process.

The alternative-catalyst choices were an autonomous factorial decision. Their identities were opaque, so there was no material-property basis for expecting one ordering over another. Before observing them, any detailed ranking was an unverified guess.

### Ethanol perturbation: Batch 11

Batch 11 showed that high conversion alone was not a sufficient process objective. Ethanol retained conversion 0.971 but reduced yield/selectivity to 0.656/0.636 and raised byproduct/degradation to 0.340/0.211. This created the solvent–branching term in K1.

The choice of ethanol, however, was only one categorical probe. I had no prior evidence that ethanol was the most informative alternative, and I did not test acetonitrile or toluene. It was therefore partly a convenience-driven guess.

### Matched unquenched run: Batch 12

Batch 12 was chosen to separate thermal arrest from an assumed chemical benefit of quenching. Its composition was close to quenched Batch 1, while terminal risk remained about 0.325 instead of falling to approximately 0.125. This narrowed the quench claim: K1 said quenching had a clear safety benefit but no resolved immediate composition benefit.

This was a hypothesis-driven experiment based on existing observations, not on the initial model. It also served as a partial repeat of the reference composition, although quench status and therefore the terminal trajectory differed.

### Choices that were weakly grounded

The failed short-time Batch 5, selection of ethanol as the only alternative solvent, omission of catalyst-loading tests, and use of only one run per alternative catalyst were not strongly justified by prior quantitative evidence. The final decision to spend the last batch on quench comparison rather than a replicate of Batch 3 improved interpretation of quenching but left the recommended condition unreplicated.

## 3. Principal competing mechanisms and what is identifiable

K1 proposed a coarse network with reactant `R`, target `P`, competing material `I`, degradation `D`, and an optional active catalyst state `C*`:

`R -> P`, `R -> I`, and `P -> D`, with catalyst-, solvent-, and temperature-dependent rates and possible catalyst deactivation.

The most important remaining competition is among the following explanations.

### A. Parallel competition plus sequential target degradation

In this account, Catalyst B favors `R -> P`, while a thermal background favors `R -> I`; accumulated `P` is subsequently lost through `P -> D`. It naturally explains the uncatalyzed control, the temperature-dependent decline in selectivity, and the poorer 4800 s result.

### B. Parallel competition with time-dependent catalyst deactivation

Here, much of the long-time loss is not destruction of already formed target. Instead, Catalyst B loses activity or changes selectivity, so late reactant conversion is increasingly routed toward impurity. This also explains the long-exposure result and could coexist with some target degradation.

### C. Reversible target formation followed by irreversible removal

Target formation could be reversible, with high temperature shifting a quasi-equilibrium or allowing irreversible impurity formation. Final snapshots could look similar to sequential degradation even if the microscopic mechanism differs.

### D. Solvent-dependent catalyst state versus solvent-dependent product stability

The ethanol result could arise because ethanol changes catalyst activity or branching, because it destabilizes target, or because it accelerates a separate degradation route. One categorical solvent comparison cannot distinguish these cases.

### What the experiments distinguish

The experiments do distinguish a catalyst-directed target route from a predominantly nonselective uncatalyzed background. Batch 10 makes a catalyst-independent, uniformly selective mechanism implausible. They also establish that excessive thermal exposure is harmful to final target yield and that temperature affects branching, not merely total conversion.

### What they do not distinguish

The experiments do not uniquely separate direct impurity formation from target degradation, catalyst deactivation, or reversibility. The midpoint HPLC measurements and final assays used different instrument contracts, so their numerical differences are not a clean same-channel kinetic time series. There were no catalyst recovery tests, no second reagent challenge, no catalyst-loading series, and no direct catalyst-state measurement. Therefore, K1’s optional deactivation term was appropriately labeled as possible rather than demonstrated.

Likewise, the data cannot support a numerical Arrhenius model. Temperature, time, ramp history, and branch composition were not varied densely enough, and the failed short-time run removed an important kinetic anchor.

## 4. One additional complete experiment I would choose

I would choose a catalyst-activity challenge designed to discriminate target degradation from Catalyst B deactivation:

1. Add 0.005 L water, 0.003 mol reagent, and 0.000525 mol Catalyst B.
2. Heat near 420 K for 3300 s at the established stirring rate.
3. Take the allowed nonfinal HPLC measurement at that point.
4. Add a second 0.003 mol reagent pulse without adding more catalyst.
5. Heat for a further valid interval, preferably 1650 s at 420 K.
6. Quench, terminate, and perform the final assay.

This would remain imperfect because the reagent concentration changes and the intermediate and final instruments differ, but it would be more discriminating than another single endpoint.

Possible outcomes would change my judgment as follows:

- **High conversion of the enlarged reagent pool with retained target selectivity:** Catalyst B remains substantially active after 3300 s. This would weaken deactivation as the dominant explanation for Batch 6 and strengthen sequential target degradation or direct thermal damage.
- **Poor incremental conversion after the second pulse:** This would support loss of catalytic activity, though reagent inhibition or altered concentration would remain alternatives.
- **Substantial additional conversion but strongly degraded selectivity:** This would support a time-dependent change in catalyst branching or accumulation of a species that promotes impurity formation.
- **Final target amount approximately preserved while the new reagent mainly becomes impurity:** This would favor a late nonselective pathway over rapid destruction of the original target.
- **Unexpectedly high target yield exceeding the reference trend:** This would suggest that concentration or staged reagent delivery changes the network and would invalidate a simple time-only degradation interpretation.

If the sole objective were validating the sealed recommendation rather than mechanism discrimination, I would instead replicate Batch 3 exactly. The challenge experiment is my choice here because the question permits only one experiment and the largest mechanistic uncertainty is deactivation versus post-formation loss.

## 5. Tradeoff between identifiability and operational score

The research goal explicitly prioritized an explanatory and predictive account over the public safe score. That materially influenced the campaign.

Experiments that sacrificed expected score for identifiability included:

- Batch 4 at approximately 430 K, which approached or crossed unsafe operation but defined the high-temperature loss of selectivity.
- Batch 6 at 4800 s, which was expected to risk overexposure and indeed scored below the best batches.
- Batches 7–10, particularly the uncatalyzed control, which were unlikely to outperform Catalyst B but were essential for identifying catalyst-directed branching.
- Batch 11 in ethanol, which tested solvent coupling at the expense of using another batch near the known high-performing water region.
- Batch 12 without quench, which deliberately accepted higher terminal risk to isolate the function of quenching.

There was nevertheless some optimization pressure. Once Batch 3 gave the best observed balance, I did not spend enough remaining capacity resolving the narrow 405–420 K region or replicating Batch 3. I also chose Catalyst B for the solvent and quench follow-ups because it was already the best catalyst. That improved the relevance of those results to the recommended process but reduced the ability to identify catalyst–solvent interactions across the full factorial space.

The recommendation itself favored score and safety balance: Batch 3 was selected rather than the most mechanistically extreme condition. Conversely, the broader campaign sacrificed potentially higher average score in order to include controls and adverse conditions. This was consistent with the stated research objective.

A further design compromise was the use of midpoint HPLC measurements in every batch. They supplied trajectory information, but because final results came from a different instrument, they did not provide the clean same-channel kinetic series needed for quantitative rate identification. A more deliberate allocation of nonfinal instruments and sampling times could have improved identifiability.

## 6. Underused evidence and weaknesses in the blind predictions

### Evidence that was difficult to exploit

The intermediate HPLC measurements were underused quantitatively. They showed sensible qualitative temperature trends, but I did not fit a joint observation model connecting HPLC and final-assay channels. Consequently, I could not reliably convert midpoint-to-final changes into rate estimates.

The detailed characterization artifacts and raw spectral packets were not inspected. K1 relied on processed estimates. Those artifacts might have exposed calibration flags, peak overlap, or additional uncertainty information, although they would not reveal hidden molecular identities.

Actual thermal telemetry was used qualitatively, but I did not reconstruct a complete exposure integral for every run. K1 correctly said that actual rather than nominal temperature should drive the model, yet the proposed equations were not fitted to the recorded ramps and holds.

Batch 1 and Batch 12 formed a useful near-replicate pair, but quench status differed. I used them to constrain the quench interpretation, not to estimate pure run-to-run variance. The absence of exact replicates remained a major limitation.

The score observations were also not modeled explicitly. In the blind predictions, score was estimated from qualitative relationships among composition, risk, and observed campaign scores rather than from an identified scoring equation.

### Least reliable blind predictions

All twelve blind predictions were structurally uncertain because every query used solvent 2, acetonitrile, which was never tested. The sealed prediction rationale admitted that I “provisionally treated acetonitrile as somewhat more selective than water.” That directional assumption was speculative and was not supported by K1. K1 explicitly limited the solvent claim to the observed water-versus-ethanol comparison and warned against general solvent-property extrapolation.

The least reliable individual predictions were:

- **Q12:** 460 K for 6300 s was far beyond the measured temperature–duration region. Its point estimates for selectivity 0.40, yield 0.40, and score 0.10 depended on extrapolating both thermal degradation and the unknown acetonitrile effect.
- **Q04:** 450 K for 3300 s extrapolated above the highest measured condition and predicted an unsafe terminal state. Its composition intervals may not cover nonlinear failure or clipping behavior.
- **Q07 and Q08:** The order effect for 390-to-450 K versus 450-to-390 K was not experimentally identified. I predicted better retained selectivity and much lower final risk for Q08, but the compositional order effect was model-based conjecture.
- **Q05, Q09, and Q10:** These involved 1500 s heat operations. Batch 5 only established that 900 s segments rolled back; it did not identify whether 1500 s operations would succeed. Their outcome distributions could be bimodal—successful heating versus rollback—whereas I reported single continuous intervals.
- **Q11:** The 370 K, 5700 s condition extrapolated below the measured temperature range while assuming duration would compensate for slower kinetics.

### Intervals that may have been too narrow

The Q01/Q02 selectivity interval of 0.68–0.94 may have been too narrow because the unknown acetonitrile category could plausibly behave worse than ethanol or interact unexpectedly with Catalyst B. The same systematic solvent uncertainty affects every query and is correlated across them; independent-looking intervals obscure that shared uncertainty.

The safety intervals for Q04 and Q12 may also have been too narrow because no experiment was conducted at 450–460 K in acetonitrile, and the thermal controller or safety model could become nonlinear there. Likewise, the score intervals inherit uncertainty from an incompletely identified scoring relationship.

These weaknesses are partly inconsistent with the strict scope stated in K1. K1 limited its supported domain to water and one ethanol comparison and explicitly said it could not infer behavior in acetonitrile. The blind task required predictions anyway, so extrapolation was unavoidable, but the point assumption that acetonitrile would improve selectivity went beyond the sealed mechanism report. The accompanying rationale disclosed that fact, yet some intervals probably did not fully represent it.

No prediction truth has been supplied at this stage, so these are prospective criticisms of the reasoning and uncertainty calibration, not retrospective explanations of observed prediction errors.

## 7. Limitations of the sealed recommendation

The sealed recommendation selected Batch 3: water, Catalyst B at 0.000525 mol, 0.003 mol reagent, actual temperature near 405 K, approximately 3300 s, followed by quenching.

Its first limitation is statistical. Batch 3 was the sample-in highest observed yield and score among the tested safe conditions, but its yield advantage over Batches 1 and 4 was within declared assay uncertainty. K1 explicitly stated that the ordering of the 405, 420, and 430 K yields was unresolved. Therefore, Batch 3 was not proven to be the unique optimum.

Its second limitation is lack of replication. There was only one Batch 3 run. Repeating the condition is necessary to estimate process variability, confirm that the measured score is reproducible, and determine whether its apparent advantage persists.

Its third limitation is sparse local coverage. A robust local validation would use replicated conditions around approximately 400–415 K and roughly 2800–3800 s, with actual thermal histories matched rather than nominal set points alone. Such a design should test whether modest controller, duration, or temperature deviations preserve conversion, selectivity, risk, and score.

Its fourth limitation is fixed composition. The recommendation did not optimize catalyst loading, reagent concentration, solvent volume, or stirring rate. Catalyst B was best at one loading, but a lower loading might retain selectivity at reduced cost, while a higher loading might shorten necessary exposure. Neither possibility was tested.

Its fifth limitation is categorical material dependence. The recommendation applies to the anonymous Catalyst B formulation and water in this benchmark. To test cross-material robustness, one would need repeated catalyst lots or formulations, controlled solvent changes, and catalyst–solvent interaction experiments. The poorer ethanol result warns against assuming transfer across solvents.

Finally, cross-world generalization is unsupported. The public materials are benchmark categories, not named chemical identities, and hidden world parameters may change between worlds. Validation across worlds would require preregistering the Batch 3 recipe and testing whether its rank, not merely its absolute yield, remains stable under new latent parameterizations.

The correct characterization is therefore: Batch 3 was the best observed local compromise in this campaign and a rational candidate for confirmation. It was not demonstrated to be globally optimal, uniquely optimal, or transferable beyond the tested benchmark context.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 3 (water, Catalyst B, about 405 K actual temperature, 3300 s, then quench) gave the best observed balance: the highest measured target yield among the safe temperature screen, strong conversion, lower byproduct/degradation and lower terminal risk than the hotter runs. The yield edge over nearby conditions is within assay uncertainty, so this is a local operating recommendation rather than a unique optimum.
